nodes.name: Sign conjugation invariance
nodes.statement: For any interaction matrix $J$, external field $h$, and diagonal matrix of signs $D$, we have: \[ \norm*{\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}}} = \norm*{\Cov\parens*{\mu_{DJD, Dh}}}\mper \] In fact, $\MLSI(\mu_{J,h}) = \MLSI(\mu_{DJD,Dh})$.
assumptions: For any interaction matrix $J$, external field $h$, and diagonal matrix of signs $D$
nodes.label: obs:sign-conjugation

nodes.name: Proof of sign conjugation invariance
nodes.statement: Note that if $\sigma\sim\mu_{J,h}$, the vector $D\sigma$ is distributed as $\mu_{DJD,Dh}$. Thus, $\Cov\parens*{\mu_{DJD,Dh}} = D\cdot\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}}\cdot D$. The first observation now follows since $D$ is an orthogonal matrix. For the second part, we have that for any function $f : \{\pm 1\}^n \to \R_{>0}$, if we define $g : \{\pm 1\}^n \to \R_{>0}$ by $g(\sigma) = f(D\sigma)$, then the entropies and Dirichlet forms of $f$ and $g$ with respect to $\mu_{J,h}$ and $\mu_{DJD,Dh}$ (respectively) are equal.
nodes.statement_short: The map $\sigma\mapsto D\sigma$ pushes $\mu_{J,h}$ to $\mu_{DJD,Dh}$ and is orthogonal.

nodes.name: Push-forward under $D$
nodes.statement: Note that if $\sigma\sim\mu_{J,h}$, the vector $D\sigma$ is distributed as $\mu_{DJD,Dh}$. Thus, $\Cov\parens*{\mu_{DJD,Dh}} = D\cdot\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}}\cdot D$.
nodes.statement_short: $D\sigma\sim\mu_{DJD,Dh}$, so Cov conjugates by $D$.

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.statement: The first observation now follows since $D$ is an orthogonal matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Norms agree since $D$ is orthogonal.

nodes.name: MLSI invariance
nodes.statement: For the second part, we have that for any function $f : \{\pm 1\}^n \to \R_{>0}$, if we define $g : \{\pm 1\}^n \to \R_{>0}$ by $g(\sigma) = f(D\sigma)$, then the entropies and Dirichlet forms of $f$ and $g$ with respect to $\mu_{J,h}$ and $\mu_{DJD,Dh}$ (respectively) are equal.
nodes.statement_short: Entropies and Dirichlet forms agree under $g(\sigma)=f(D\sigma)$.

nodes.name: Gauge transform to nonnegative tree interactions
nodes.statement: For any connected graph $H$ and spanning tree $T$ of $H$, interaction matrix $J$ supported on $H$, and an external field $h$, there is a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $DJD$ has nonnegative interactions on the edges of $T$.
assumptions: For any connected graph $H$ and spanning tree $T$ of $H$, interaction matrix $J$ supported on $H$, and an external field $h$
conclusions: there is a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $DJD$ has nonnegative interactions on the edges of $T$
nodes.label: lem:all-but-one-neg

nodes.name: Proof of the gauge transform lemma
nodes.statement: Arbitrarily root $T$ at a vertex $r$. Construct $D$ by choosing $D_{v,v} = \prod_{e'\in P} \sign(J_{e'})$ where $P$ is the unique path from $r$ to $v$ in $T$. For any edge $uv\in E(T)$, $(DJD)_{u,v} = J_{u,v} D_{u,u} D_{v,v} = J_{u,v} \sign\parens*{J_{u,v}} \ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $D$ from products of signs along root-to-vertex tree paths.

nodes.name: Construct $D$
nodes.statement: Arbitrarily root $T$ at a vertex $r$. Construct $D$ by choosing $D_{v,v} = \prod_{e'\in P} \sign(J_{e'})$ where $P$ is the unique path from $r$ to $v$ in $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Root $T$ and set $D_{vv}$ as the sign product along the root path.

nodes.name: Check tree edges
nodes.statement: For any edge $uv\in E(T)$, $(DJD)_{u,v} = J_{u,v} D_{u,u} D_{v,v} = J_{u,v} \sign\parens*{J_{u,v}} \ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Each tree edge gets interaction $|J_{uv}|\ge0$.

nodes.name: External fields decrease ferromagnetic covariances
nodes.statement: For any ferromagnetic interaction matrix $J\in\R_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}$ and external field $h\in\R^n$, we have for any $u,v\in[n]$: \[ \Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}}_{u,v} \le \Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,0}}_{u,v}. \]
assumptions: For any ferromagnetic interaction matrix $J\in\R_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}$ and external field $h\in\R^n$
nodes.label: lem:cov-ferro-external

nodes.name: Nonnegative correlations in ferromagnetic Ising models
nodes.statement: For any ferromagnetic interaction matrix $J \in \R_{\ge 0}^{n \times n}$, external field $h \in \R^n$, and $u,v \in [n]$, $\Cov\left( \mu_{J,h} \right)_{u,v} \ge 0$.
assumptions: For any ferromagnetic interaction matrix $J \in \R_{\ge 0}^{n \times n}$, external field $h \in \R^n$, and $u,v \in [n]$
nodes.label: fact:ferro-nonneg-correlation

nodes.name: Proof of nonnegative ferromagnetic correlations
nodes.statement: Ferromagnetic Ising models with arbitrary external fields satisfy the hypothesis of the FKG inequality \cite[Theorem 2.16]{gri06}. The statement then follows from the FKG inequality applied to the functions $\sigma_i - \E[\sigma_i]$ and $\sigma_j - \E[\sigma_j]$.
nodes.statement_short: FKG inequality applied to centered spins.

nodes.name: Ferromagnetic covariance norm bound at zero field
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a matrix with all non-negative entries. For any ferromagnetic interaction matrix $J\in\R_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}$ and external field $h\in\R^n$, we have \[ \left\|\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}} \cdot M\right\| \le \left\|\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,0}} \cdot M\right\|. \] In particular, \[ \left\|\Cov(\mu_{J,h})\right\| \le \left\|\Cov(\mu_{J,0})\right\|. \]
assumptions: Let $M$ be a matrix with all non-negative entries.
For any ferromagnetic interaction matrix $J\in\R_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}$ and external field $h\in\R^n$
nodes.label: cor:cov-ferro-external-psd

nodes.name: Proof of the ferromagnetic covariance norm bound
nodes.statement: This is immediate by \Cref{fact:ferro-nonneg-correlation,lem:cov-ferro-external}, and the Perron-Frobenius theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Entrywise domination of nonnegative matrices plus Perron-Frobenius.

nodes.name: Trace-method norm bounds for distance matrices on pseudorandom trees
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree with respect to $S \subseteq V(H)$. Let $\ell \ge 1$, and set $A^{(\ell)} = A^{(\ell)}_H$ to be the matrix with $(A^{(\ell)})_{uv} = 1$ if vertices $u$ and $v$ are distance exactly $\ell$ apart, and $0$ otherwise. Also let $A = A^{(1)}$ be the adjacency matrix of $H$. Then, \begin{align*} \left\| A^{(\ell)} \right\| &\le D^{\ell/2} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot \left( \frac{\Delta}{D} \right) \\ \left\| A^{(\ell)}_S \right\| &\le D^{\ell/2} \cdot (\ell+1) \\ \left\| A^{(\ell)} A \right\| &\le D^{\ell/2} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot \left( \frac{2\Delta}{\sqrt{D}} \right) \mper \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree with respect to $S \subseteq V(H)$.
Let $\ell \ge 1$, and set $A^{(\ell)} = A^{(\ell)}_H$ to be the matrix with $(A^{(\ell)})_{uv} = 1$ if vertices $u$ and $v$ are distance exactly $\ell$ apart, and $0$ otherwise.
Also let $A = A^{(1)}$ be the adjacency matrix of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Distance-$\ell$ matrices of pseudorandom trees have norm $\lesssim D^{\ell/2}(\ell+1)$ times $\Delta/D$, 1, or $2\Delta/\sqrt D$.
nodes.label: lem:trace-method-best-method

nodes.name: Trace moment proof of distance-matrix norm bounds
nodes.statement: We shall bound these operator norms using the trace moment method. Let $R$ be $S$ or $V(H)$, so we are interested in bounding $\left\|A^{(\ell)}_R\right\|$. Let us define $\calW_{\ell,m,R}$ to be the set of all closed walks in $H$ of length $\ell\cdot m$ that can be expressed as the concatenation of $m$ nonbacktracking walks\footnote{In a tree, nonbacktracking walks are equivalent to shortest paths.} between a pair of vertices in $R$ of length-$\ell$ each. Henceforth, we refer to each of these length-$\ell$ nonbacktracking walks as a \emph{linkage}. For any even integer $m > 0$, we have: \[ \left\| A^{(\ell)}_R \right\|^m \le \Tr\parens*{ \parens*{A^{(\ell)}_R}^m } = \abs*{\calW_{\ell,m,R}}. \] For each vertex $r\in R$, we count the number of walks that start and end at $r$. The $t$-th linkage, if started at a vertex $v$, is composed of $s_t$ steps ``upwards'' away from $v$, followed by $\ell-s_t$ steps ``downwards''. Since $H$ is a tree, and the walks we are counting start and end at the same vertex, exactly half of the steps in any walk are upwards, and exactly half are downwards, that is, $$ \sum_{t=1}^m s_t = \sum_{t=1}^m \ell-s_t = \ell\cdot m / 2\mper $$ Given $s_t$, the number of choices for the $t$-th linkage is at most $D^{\ell-s_t-1} \cdot \Delta_R$ where $\Delta_R$ is $D$ when $R = S$ and $\Delta$ when $R = V(H)$. \[ \abs*{\calW_{\ell,m,R}} \le |R| \cdot \sum_{s_1,\dots,s_{m}} \prod_{t=1}^m D^{\ell-s_t}\cdot\frac{\Delta_R}{D} = |R| \cdot \sum_{s_1,\dots,s_m} D^{\ell\cdot m / 2} \cdot \parens*{\frac{\Delta_R}{D}}^m \le |R| \cdot D^{\ell\cdot m / 2} \cdot \parens*{\frac{\Delta_R}{D}}^m \cdot (\ell+1)^m \mper \] Thus, taking $m \to \infty$ so $|R|^{1/m} \to 1$, we get that \[ \norm*{ A^{(\ell)}_R } \le D^{\ell/2} \cdot \left( \frac{\Delta_R}{D} \right) \cdot (\ell+1). \] The first two inequalities follow by plugging in $\Delta_S = D$ and $\Delta_{V(H)} = \Delta$.\\ The proof of the third inequality is very similar. The main difference is that each of the linkages is not a length-$\ell$ nonbacktracking walk, but instead a length-$(\ell+1)$ walk, of which the first $\ell$ steps are non-backtracking. That is, the $t$-th ``linkage'' is now composed of $s_t$ steps upwards, followed by $\ell-s_t$ steps downwards, followed by a single step upwards or downwards. If the final step is downwards, this is just $s_t$ steps upwards then $\ell - s_t + 1$ steps downwards. If the final step is upwards, then this can be thought of as changing $s_{t+1}$ to $s_{t+1} + 1$. We encode this with $\eps_t, \eps'_t \in \{0,1\}$, wherein the $t$-th linkage consists of $s_t + \eps_t$ steps upwards followed by $\ell - s_t + \eps'_t$ steps downwards. Since $\eps'_t+\eps_{t+1}=1$, the sequence $(\eps'_t)$ is determined by $(\eps_t)$, and $\sum \eps_t + \eps'_t = m$. Consequently, \[ \sum_{t} s_t + \eps_t = \sum_{t} \ell - s_t + \eps'_t = \frac{(\ell+1)m}{2}\mper \] Setting $\mathcal{W}'_{\ell,m}$ as the set of walks enumerated by this trace moment method calculation,\footnote{In this case, $R$ is fixed to be $V(H)$.} we have \begin{align*} |\mathcal{W}'_{\ell,m}| &\le V(H) \cdot \sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_m,\eps_1,\ldots,\eps_m} \prod_{t=1}^{m} D^{\ell - s_t + \eps'_t} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D} \\ &= V(H) \cdot \sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_m,\eps_1,\ldots,\eps_m} D^{(\ell+1)m/2} \cdot \left(\frac{\Delta}{D}\right)^m \\ &\le V(H) \cdot (\ell+1)^m \cdot 2^m \cdot D^{(\ell+1)m/2} \cdot \left( \frac{\Delta}{D} \right)^m. \end{align*} Again, taking $m\to\infty$ so $V(H)^{1/m} \to 1$, we get that \[ \left\| A^{(\ell)} A \right\| \le D^{(\ell+1)/2} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D} \cdot 2 (\ell+1) \] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Trace moment method: count closed walks made of $m$ length-$\ell$ linkages using the ball-growth bounds. The third bound handles one extra step per linkage via $\eps_t,\eps'_t$ bookkeeping.

nodes.name: Trace moment setup
nodes.statement: We shall bound these operator norms using the trace moment method. Let $R$ be $S$ or $V(H)$, so we are interested in bounding $\left\|A^{(\ell)}_R\right\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the trace moment method for $R\in\{S,V(H)\}$.

nodes.name: Define linkage walks
nodes.statement: Let us define $\calW_{\ell,m,R}$ to be the set of all closed walks in $H$ of length $\ell\cdot m$ that can be expressed as the concatenation of $m$ nonbacktracking walks\footnote{In a tree, nonbacktracking walks are equivalent to shortest paths.} between a pair of vertices in $R$ of length-$\ell$ each. Henceforth, we refer to each of these length-$\ell$ nonbacktracking walks as a \emph{linkage}.
nodes.statement_short: Closed walks made of $m$ length-$\ell$ nonbacktracking linkages.

nodes.name: Norm by trace
nodes.statement: For any even integer $m > 0$, we have: \[ \left\| A^{(\ell)}_R \right\|^m \le \Tr\parens*{ \parens*{A^{(\ell)}_R}^m } = \abs*{\calW_{\ell,m,R}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\|A^{(\ell)}_R\|^m\le$ number of such walks.

nodes.name: Up/down step structure
nodes.statement: For each vertex $r\in R$, we count the number of walks that start and end at $r$. The $t$-th linkage, if started at a vertex $v$, is composed of $s_t$ steps ``upwards'' away from $v$, followed by $\ell-s_t$ steps ``downwards''. Since $H$ is a tree, and the walks we are counting start and end at the same vertex, exactly half of the steps in any walk are upwards, and exactly half are downwards, that is, $$ \sum_{t=1}^m s_t = \sum_{t=1}^m \ell-s_t = \ell\cdot m / 2\mper $$
nodes.statement_short: Half the steps of each closed walk in a tree go up.

nodes.name: Count walks
nodes.statement: Given $s_t$, the number of choices for the $t$-th linkage is at most $D^{\ell-s_t-1} \cdot \Delta_R$ where $\Delta_R$ is $D$ when $R = S$ and $\Delta$ when $R = V(H)$. \[ \abs*{\calW_{\ell,m,R}} \le |R| \cdot \sum_{s_1,\dots,s_{m}} \prod_{t=1}^m D^{\ell-s_t}\cdot\frac{\Delta_R}{D} = |R| \cdot \sum_{s_1,\dots,s_m} D^{\ell\cdot m / 2} \cdot \parens*{\frac{\Delta_R}{D}}^m \le |R| \cdot D^{\ell\cdot m / 2} \cdot \parens*{\frac{\Delta_R}{D}}^m \cdot (\ell+1)^m \mper \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound the walk count via ball growth.

nodes.name: Take $m\to\infty$
nodes.statement: Thus, taking $m \to \infty$ so $|R|^{1/m} \to 1$, we get that \[ \norm*{ A^{(\ell)}_R } \le D^{\ell/2} \cdot \left( \frac{\Delta_R}{D} \right) \cdot (\ell+1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Get $\|A^{(\ell)}_R\|\le D^{\ell/2}(\Delta_R/D)(\ell+1)$.

nodes.name: First two bounds
nodes.statement: The first two inequalities follow by plugging in $\Delta_S = D$ and $\Delta_{V(H)} = \Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Plug in $\Delta_S=D$ and $\Delta_{V(H)}=\Delta$.

nodes.name: Third bound: modified linkages
nodes.statement: The proof of the third inequality is very similar. The main difference is that each of the linkages is not a length-$\ell$ nonbacktracking walk, but instead a length-$(\ell+1)$ walk, of which the first $\ell$ steps are non-backtracking. That is, the $t$-th ``linkage'' is now composed of $s_t$ steps upwards, followed by $\ell-s_t$ steps downwards, followed by a single step upwards or downwards. If the final step is downwards, this is just $s_t$ steps upwards then $\ell - s_t + 1$ steps downwards. If the final step is upwards, then this can be thought of as changing $s_{t+1}$ to $s_{t+1} + 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Linkages now have one extra step, up or down.

nodes.name: Encode extra steps
nodes.statement: We encode this with $\eps_t, \eps'_t \in \{0,1\}$, wherein the $t$-th linkage consists of $s_t + \eps_t$ steps upwards followed by $\ell - s_t + \eps'_t$ steps downwards. Since $\eps'_t+\eps_{t+1}=1$, the sequence $(\eps'_t)$ is determined by $(\eps_t)$, and $\sum \eps_t + \eps'_t = m$. Consequently, \[ \sum_{t} s_t + \eps_t = \sum_{t} \ell - s_t + \eps'_t = \frac{(\ell+1)m}{2}\mper \]
nodes.statement_short: Track extra steps with $\eps_t,\eps'_t$.

nodes.name: Count modified walks
nodes.statement: Setting $\mathcal{W}'_{\ell,m}$ as the set of walks enumerated by this trace moment method calculation,\footnote{In this case, $R$ is fixed to be $V(H)$.} we have \begin{align*} |\mathcal{W}'_{\ell,m}| &\le V(H) \cdot \sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_m,\eps_1,\ldots,\eps_m} \prod_{t=1}^{m} D^{\ell - s_t + \eps'_t} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D} \\ &= V(H) \cdot \sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_m,\eps_1,\ldots,\eps_m} D^{(\ell+1)m/2} \cdot \left(\frac{\Delta}{D}\right)^m \\ &\le V(H) \cdot (\ell+1)^m \cdot 2^m \cdot D^{(\ell+1)m/2} \cdot \left( \frac{\Delta}{D} \right)^m. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the number of modified walks.

nodes.name: Third bound
nodes.statement: Again, taking $m\to\infty$ so $V(H)^{1/m} \to 1$, we get that \[ \left\| A^{(\ell)} A \right\| \le D^{(\ell+1)/2} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D} \cdot 2 (\ell+1) \] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\|A^{(\ell)}A\|$ bound.

nodes.name: Covariance bounds for ferromagnetic tree Ising models at zero field
assumptions: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree with respect to $S\subseteq V(H)$.
Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of $H$.
If $J$ is a collection of interactions supported on the edges of $H$ with values in $\bracks*{0, \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}}$ for some $\gamma \in [0,1)$
nodes.statement_short: Zero-field ferromagnetic tree Ising covariances are bounded by $(1-\gamma)^{-2}$ times $1$, $\Delta/D$, or $2\Delta/\sqrt D$.
nodes.label: lem:tree-cov

nodes.name: Proof of tree covariance bounds
nodes.statement_short: Write the covariance as a sum of path-product matrices, dominate entrywise by $(\gamma/\sqrt D)^\ell$ distance matrices, and apply the trace-method bounds.

nodes.name: Explicit covariance formula
nodes.statement: We start with the first two bounds, using the following explicit formula for the covariance matrix. \[ \Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,0}} = \sum_{\ell\ge 0} X^{(\ell)}, \] where $X^{(\ell)}_{i,j}$ is $0$ if there is no length-$\ell$ path between $i$ and $j$ in $H$, and is otherwise equal to $\prod_{e\in P(i,j)} \tanh(J_e)$ where $P(i,j)$ is the unique such path.
nodes.statement_short: Covariance equals the sum of path-product matrices $X^{(\ell)}$.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: For $R\subseteq V(H)$, will use the bound: \begin{equation} \norm*{\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,0}}_R} \le \sum_{\ell\ge 0} \norm*{X^{(\ell)}_R}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound by the sum of norms of $X^{(\ell)}_R$.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality bound on restricted covariance
nodes.statement: \norm*{\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,0}}_R} \le \sum_{\ell\ge 0} \norm*{X^{(\ell)}_R}.
nodes.label: eq:trace-moment-cov-bound-ez

nodes.name: Entrywise domination
nodes.statement: Consider the matrix $Y^{(\ell)}$ obtained by replacing each nonzero entry of $X^{(\ell)}$ with $\parens*{\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}}^{\ell}$. Since the interactions are all nonnegative, $X^{(\ell)}$ is a nonnegative matrix, and $Y^{(\ell)}$ is entrywise at least $X^{(\ell)}$ since $\tanh(x) \le x$ for $x \ge 0$. Consequently, \begin{equation} \norm*{X^{(\ell)}_R} \le \norm*{Y^{(\ell)}_R}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Replace entries by $(\gamma/\sqrt D)^\ell$ using $\tanh x\le x$.

nodes.name: Termwise domination bound
nodes.statement: \norm*{X^{(\ell)}_R} \le \norm*{Y^{(\ell)}_R}.
nodes.label: eq:trace-moment-termwise-bound-ez

nodes.name: Apply trace-method bounds
nodes.statement: \Cref{lem:trace-method-best-method} now implies that \[ \norm*{Y^{(\ell)}_R} \le \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)^{\ell} \cdot D^{\ell/2} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot \left(\frac{\Delta_R}{D}\right) = \gamma^{\ell} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot \left(\frac{\Delta_R}{D}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Each term is $\gamma^\ell(\ell+1)\Delta_R/D$.

nodes.name: Sum the series (first two bounds)
nodes.statement: Therefore, \[ \norm*{\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,0}}_R} \le \frac{\Delta_R}{D} \cdot \sum_{\ell \ge 0} (\ell+1) \gamma^{\ell} \le \frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^2}\cdot\frac{\Delta_R}{D}\mcom \] which recovers the desired bounds by plugging in $\Delta_R = \Delta$ for $R = V(H)$, and $\Delta_R = D$ for $R=S$.
nodes.statement_short: Summing gives $(1-\gamma)^{-2}\Delta_R/D$.

nodes.name: Third bound setup
nodes.statement:
For the third inequality, we again have \[ \Cov\left(\mu_{J,0}ight)\cdot A = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} 
orm*{X^{(\ell)} \cdot A}. \] Again, the non-negativity of $X^{(\ell)}$ and $A$ implies that \[ 
orm*{X^{(\ell)} \cdot A} \le 
orm*{Y^{(\ell)} \cdot A}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand Cov$\cdot A$ and dominate termwise.

nodes.name: Apply third trace bound
nodes.statement: The third bound in \Cref{lem:trace-method-best-method} now implies that \begin{align*} \norm*{Y^{(\ell)} \cdot A} &\le \left(\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}\right)^{\ell} D^{(\ell+1)/2} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot 2 \cdot \left( \frac{\Delta}{D} \right) \\ &= \gamma^{\ell} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{D}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Each term is $2\gamma^\ell(\ell+1)\Delta/\sqrt D$.

nodes.name: Sum the series (third bound)
nodes.statement: Therefore, \[ \norm*{\Cov\left(\mu_{J,0}\right) \cdot A} \le \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \gamma^{\ell} \cdot (\ell+1) \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{D}} \le \frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^2} \cdot \frac{2\Delta}{\sqrt{D}}, \] completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Summing gives the third bound.

nodes.name: Proof of the near-forest covariance bound
nodes.statement: The matrix $\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}}$ is a block diagonal matrix with a block per connected component of $H$, and so without loss of generality, it suffices to achieve a bound on the spectral norm in the case where $H$ is a connected near-forest (a near-tree) --- a tree with possibly one extra edge inserted. If $H$ has tree-excess $0$, the desideratum is trivial by \Cref{fact:ferro-nonneg-correlation,lem:cov-ferro-external,lem:tree-cov}. Hence, let us assume that $H$ has tree-excess $1$. Let $T$ be an arbitrary ($(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom) spanning tree of $H$, such that the edge set of $H$ consists of those in $T$ along with an extra edge $ij$. By \Cref{obs:sign-conjugation} and \Cref{lem:all-but-one-neg}, it suffices to consider the case where $J$ has nonnegative interactions on all edges in $T$, and possibly a negative interaction on $ij$. Also let $J'$ be the interaction matrix which is identical to $J$ except that $J'_{ij} =J'_{ji} = 0$. Note that $\left|\sigma^\top J \sigma - \sigma^\top J' \sigma\right| \le \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}$ for any $\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}^n$. Let $R$ be equal to $S$ or $V(H)$, with $\Delta_S = D$ and $\Delta_{V(H)} = \Delta$, and set $v$ to be a unit vector that witnesses the operator norm of $\Cov(\mu_{J,h})_{R}$. Then, \begin{align*} \|\Cov\left( \mu_{J,h} \right)_R\| &= v^\top \Cov\left( \mu_{J,h} \right) v \\ &= \Var_{\sigma \sim \mu_{J,h}}(\langle v,\sigma\rangle) \tag*{(\text{\Cref{fact:var-cov}})} \\ &\le e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}} \cdot \Var_{\sigma \sim \mu_{J',h}} (\langle v,\sigma\rangle) \tag*{(\text{\Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate}})} \\ &\le e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}} \cdot \| \Cov\left( \mu_{J',h} \right)_R \| \tag*{(\text{\Cref{fact:var-cov}})} \\ &\le e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}} \cdot \| \Cov\left( \mu_{J',0} \right)_R \| \tag*{(\text{\Cref{cor:cov-ferro-external-psd}})} \\ &\le \frac{e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}}}{(1-\gamma)^2} \cdot \frac{\Delta_R}{D} \tag*{(\text{\Cref{lem:tree-cov}})} \end{align*} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a connected near-tree, gauge to nonnegative tree interactions, drop the extra edge via Holley-Stroock, and apply the tree covariance bound.

nodes.name: Reduce to a connected near-tree
nodes.statement: The matrix $\Cov\parens*{\mu_{J,h}}$ is a block diagonal matrix with a block per connected component of $H$, and so without loss of generality, it suffices to achieve a bound on the spectral norm in the case where $H$ is a connected near-forest (a near-tree) --- a tree with possibly one extra edge inserted.
nodes.statement_short: Block structure reduces to one component.

nodes.name: Tree case
nodes.statement: If $H$ has tree-excess $0$, the desideratum is trivial by \Cref{fact:ferro-nonneg-correlation,lem:cov-ferro-external,lem:tree-cov}.
nodes.statement_short: Tree case follows from the ferromagnetic and tree covariance bounds.

nodes.name: Tree-excess one case: gauge
nodes.statement: Hence, let us assume that $H$ has tree-excess $1$. Let $T$ be an arbitrary ($(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom) spanning tree of $H$, such that the edge set of $H$ consists of those in $T$ along with an extra edge $ij$. By \Cref{obs:sign-conjugation} and \Cref{lem:all-but-one-neg}, it suffices to consider the case where $J$ has nonnegative interactions on all edges in $T$, and possibly a negative interaction on $ij$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume one extra edge; gauge the spanning tree to nonnegative interactions.

nodes.name: Remove the extra edge
nodes.statement: Also let $J'$ be the interaction matrix which is identical to $J$ except that $J'_{ij} =J'_{ji} = 0$. Note that $\left|\sigma^\top J \sigma - \sigma^\top J' \sigma\right| \le \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}$ for any $\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $J'$ without the extra edge; energies differ by at most $\gamma/\sqrt D$.

nodes.name: Chain of variance comparisons
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be equal to $S$ or $V(H)$, with $\Delta_S = D$ and $\Delta_{V(H)} = \Delta$, and set $v$ to be a unit vector that witnesses the operator norm of $\Cov(\mu_{J,h})_{R}$. Then, \begin{align*} \|\Cov\left( \mu_{J,h} \right)_R\| &= v^\top \Cov\left( \mu_{J,h} \right) v \\ &= \Var_{\sigma \sim \mu_{J,h}}(\langle v,\sigma\rangle) \tag*{(\text{\Cref{fact:var-cov}})} \\ &\le e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}} \cdot \Var_{\sigma \sim \mu_{J',h}} (\langle v,\sigma\rangle) \tag*{(\text{\Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate}})} \\ &\le e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}} \cdot \| \Cov\left( \mu_{J',h} \right)_R \| \tag*{(\text{\Cref{fact:var-cov}})} \\ &\le e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}} \cdot \| \Cov\left( \mu_{J',0} \right)_R \| \tag*{(\text{\Cref{cor:cov-ferro-external-psd}})} \\ &\le \frac{e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}}}{(1-\gamma)^2} \cdot \frac{\Delta_R}{D} \tag*{(\text{\Cref{lem:tree-cov}})} \end{align*} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Compare variances via Holley-Stroock and apply the tree bound.

nodes.name: Proof of entropy conservation for near-forest decompositions
nodes.statement: Let $\rho > 0$ be a positive constant that we fix later. We use \Cref{lem:interaction-sum-cov-bound}, with the instantiation \[ M_1 = (1-t) J_B + \frac{t}{2}I_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \text{ and } M_2 = J_H. \] Since $\eta I_B \psdle (1-t) J_B + \frac{t}{2}I_B \psdle K I_B$, we can reduce to the case where $t=0$. Now, set $\delta' = \delta/2$. For $t=0$ and an arbitrary external field $h'$, we have \begin{align*} M_1 \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot M_1 &= \left( J_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \right) \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot \left( J_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \right) \\ &\psdle \left( 1 + \delta' \right) \cdot J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B + \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\delta'} \right) \cdot \frac{\rho^2}{\Delta^2} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot I_{H \setminus \partial H} \\ &= \left(1 + \delta'\right) J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B + \left(1 + \frac{1}{\delta'}\right) \cdot \frac{\rho^2}{\Delta^2} \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H}. \end{align*} Above, the inequality follows from the observation that for symmetric matrices $A_1,A_2$, a positive semidefinite matrix $M$, and any $\alpha > 0$, \[ (A_1 + A_2) M (A_1 + A_2) \psdle \left(1+\alpha\right) A_1 M A_1 + \left(1 + \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) A_2 M A_2. \] We now make the crucial observation that we can restrict the covariance to the bulk in the first term, that is, \[ J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B = J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_B \cdot J_B. \] Indeed, observe that $(J_B)_{ij}$ must be zero for any $i,j$ where $i$ or $j$ lies in $H \setminus \partial H$, the interior of the near-forest. In particular, any such $i$ or $j$ is not in the bulk. We are interested in showing the positive definiteness of \[ \left(J_B - (1+\delta') \cdot J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_B \cdot J_B\right) + \frac{\rho}{\Delta}\left( I_{H \setminus \partial H} - \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\delta'}\right) \cdot \frac{\rho}{\Delta} \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H} \right). \] Note that had we not added the extra $(\rho/\Delta) I_H$ when defining $M_1$, the second term above would be absent, making the matrix entries zero on the rows and columns $V'(H) \setminus V'(B)$, which precludes a meaningful lower bound by a full-rank matrix.\\ By assumption, $M_2$ is supported on a $(\Delta, D)$-pseudorandom near-forest, and the interaction strengths are in $\left[ -\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} , \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right]$. Furthermore, since $\gamma < 1$, the first part of \Cref{lem:near-forest-cov} yields \begin{align*} \left\| \Cov\left( \mu_{M_2,h'} \right)_B \right\| \le \frac{e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}}}{(1-\gamma)^2} \eqdef f(\gamma). \end{align*} Consequently, \Cref{prop:prop-hs-trick} and the assumption on $\gamma$ shows that \begin{align*} J_B - \left( 1 + \delta' \right) \cdot J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B &\psdge \eta \cdot \left(1 - \left( 1 + \delta' \right) K f(\gamma)\right) I_B \\ &\psdge \eta \cdot \delta' \cdot I_B. \end{align*} Similarly, the second part of \Cref{lem:near-forest-cov} shows that \[ \left\|\Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H}\right\| \le \left\|\Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H}\right\| \le \frac{\Delta}{D} \cdot f(\gamma). \] Selecting $\rho \coloneqq \frac{D}{2 f(\gamma) \cdot \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\delta'} \right)}$, we see that \[ I_{H \setminus \partial H} - \left(1 + \frac{1}{\delta'}\right) \cdot \frac{\rho}{\Delta} \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H} \psdge \frac{1}{2} I_{H \setminus \partial H}. \] Thus, we have that \begin{align*} M_1 - M_1 \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot M_1 &\psdge \eta \delta' \cdot I_B + \frac{\rho}{2\Delta} \cdot I_{H \setminus \partial H} \\ &\psdge c\left(I_B + \frac{1}{\Delta}I_{H \setminus \partial H}\right), \end{align*} for some universal constant $c$ (that does not depend on $\Delta$). The claim follows by applying \Cref{lem:interaction-sum-cov-bound} and setting $C = c^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the sum covariance bound with $M_1=J_B+\frac{\rho}{\Delta}I_{H\setminus\partial H}$, split the quadratic form, and lower bound each block using the near-forest covariance bounds. The key step restricts the covariance to the bulk because $J_B$ vanishes on the near-forest interior.

nodes.name: Instantiate the sum covariance lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\rho > 0$ be a positive constant that we fix later. We use \Cref{lem:interaction-sum-cov-bound}, with the instantiation \[ M_1 = (1-t) J_B + \frac{t}{2}I_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \text{ and } M_2 = J_H. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use $M_1=(1-t)J_B+\frac t2I_B+\frac\rho\Delta I_{H\setminus\partial H}$, $M_2=J_H$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $t=0$
nodes.statement: Since $\eta I_B \psdle (1-t) J_B + \frac{t}{2}I_B \psdle K I_B$, we can reduce to the case where $t=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The bulk part stays between $\eta I_B$ and $KI_B$.

nodes.name: Split the quadratic form
nodes.statement: Now, set $\delta' = \delta/2$. For $t=0$ and an arbitrary external field $h'$, we have \begin{align*} M_1 \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot M_1 &= \left( J_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \right) \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot \left( J_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \right) \\ &\psdle \left( 1 + \delta' \right) \cdot J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B + \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\delta'} \right) \cdot \frac{\rho^2}{\Delta^2} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot I_{H \setminus \partial H} \\ &= \left(1 + \delta'\right) J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B + \left(1 + \frac{1}{\delta'}\right) \cdot \frac{\rho^2}{\Delta^2} \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $M_1\Cov M_1$ by weighted bulk and interior terms.

nodes.name: Matrix AM-GM inequality
nodes.statement: Above, the inequality follows from the observation that for symmetric matrices $A_1,A_2$, a positive semidefinite matrix $M$, and any $\alpha > 0$, \[ (A_1 + A_2) M (A_1 + A_2) \psdle \left(1+\alpha\right) A_1 M A_1 + \left(1 + \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) A_2 M A_2. \]
nodes.statement_short: $(A_1+A_2)M(A_1+A_2)\preceq(1+\alpha)A_1MA_1+(1+1/\alpha)A_2MA_2$.

nodes.name: Restrict covariance to the bulk
nodes.statement: We now make the crucial observation that we can restrict the covariance to the bulk in the first term, that is, \[ J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B = J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_B \cdot J_B. \] Indeed, observe that $(J_B)_{ij}$ must be zero for any $i,j$ where $i$ or $j$ lies in $H \setminus \partial H$, the interior of the near-forest. In particular, any such $i$ or $j$ is not in the bulk.
nodes.statement_short: $J_B$ vanishes on the near-forest interior, so only Cov$_B$ matters.

nodes.name: Target matrix
nodes.statement: We are interested in showing the positive definiteness of \[ \left(J_B - (1+\delta') \cdot J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_B \cdot J_B\right) + \frac{\rho}{\Delta}\left( I_{H \setminus \partial H} - \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\delta'}\right) \cdot \frac{\rho}{\Delta} \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H} \right). \] Note that had we not added the extra $(\rho/\Delta) I_H$ when defining $M_1$, the second term above would be absent, making the matrix entries zero on the rows and columns $V'(H) \setminus V'(B)$, which precludes a meaningful lower bound by a full-rank matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Need positive definiteness of a bulk term plus an interior term.

nodes.name: Bulk covariance bound
nodes.statement: By assumption, $M_2$ is supported on a $(\Delta, D)$-pseudorandom near-forest, and the interaction strengths are in $\left[ -\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} , \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right]$. Furthermore, since $\gamma < 1$, the first part of \Cref{lem:near-forest-cov} yields \begin{align*} \left\| \Cov\left( \mu_{M_2,h'} \right)_B \right\| \le \frac{e^{2\gamma/\sqrt{D}}}{(1-\gamma)^2} \eqdef f(\gamma). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Near-forest covariance lemma bounds Cov$_B$ by $f(\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Bulk term lower bound
nodes.statement: Consequently, \Cref{prop:prop-hs-trick} and the assumption on $\gamma$ shows that \begin{align*} J_B - \left( 1 + \delta' \right) \cdot J_B \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot J_B &\psdge \eta \cdot \left(1 - \left( 1 + \delta' \right) K f(\gamma)\right) I_B \\ &\psdge \eta \cdot \delta' \cdot I_B. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bulk term $\succeq\eta\delta' I_B$.

nodes.name: Interior covariance bound
nodes.statement: Similarly, the second part of \Cref{lem:near-forest-cov} shows that \[ \left\|\Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H}\right\| \le \left\|\Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H}\right\| \le \frac{\Delta}{D} \cdot f(\gamma). \]
nodes.statement_short: Interior covariance is at most $(\Delta/D)f(\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Choose $\rho$
nodes.statement: Selecting $\rho \coloneqq \frac{D}{2 f(\gamma) \cdot \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\delta'} \right)}$, we see that \[ I_{H \setminus \partial H} - \left(1 + \frac{1}{\delta'}\right) \cdot \frac{\rho}{\Delta} \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_{H \setminus \partial H} \psdge \frac{1}{2} I_{H \setminus \partial H}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\rho$ so the interior term is $\succeq\frac12I$.

nodes.name: Combined lower bound
nodes.statement: Thus, we have that \begin{align*} M_1 - M_1 \cdot \Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'}) \cdot M_1 &\psdge \eta \delta' \cdot I_B + \frac{\rho}{2\Delta} \cdot I_{H \setminus \partial H} \\ &\psdge c\left(I_B + \frac{1}{\Delta}I_{H \setminus \partial H}\right), \end{align*} for some universal constant $c$ (that does not depend on $\Delta$).
nodes.statement_short: $M_1-M_1\Cov M_1\succeq c(I_B+\Delta^{-1}I_{H\setminus\partial H})$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The claim follows by applying \Cref{lem:interaction-sum-cov-bound} and setting $C = c^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the sum covariance lemma with $C=c^{-1}$.

nodes.name: MLSI for ferromagnetic Ising models on pseudorandom trees
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree on $n$ vertices, and $J$ an interaction matrix supported on $H$ with all interactions in $\left[0, \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}\right]$ for some $\gamma \in [0,1)$. There is a constant $c$ (depending on $\gamma$) such that for any external field $h \in \R^n$, \[ \MLSI(\mu_{J,h}) \ge \frac{1}{ne^{c\Delta}}\mper \]
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
assumptions: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree on $n$ vertices, and $J$ an interaction matrix supported on $H$ with all interactions in $\left[0, \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}\right]$ for some $\gamma \in [0,1)$.
conclusions: There is a constant $c$ (depending on $\gamma$) such that for any external field $h \in \R^n$, \[ \MLSI(\mu_{J,h}) \ge \frac{1}{ne^{c\Delta}}\mper \]
nodes.label: lem:pseudorandom-ferro-mixing

nodes.name: Broader interaction range and optimality conjecture
nodes.statement: In fact, our proof works in a slightly broader range of the interactions, only requiring that for some $\gamma \in [0,1)$, all the interactions are bounded (in absolute value) by $\tanh^{-1} \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)$. We conjecture that this is optimal.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests

nodes.name: Proof of tree MLSI with equal interactions (Bethe Hessian control matrix)
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Stochastic localization with control matrix $C=((1-s_0^2)\BH(-s_0))^{1/2}$, which cancels the large part of the covariance $\BH(s_0)^{-1}$. The key identity is $\BH(s_0)^{-1}\BH(-s_0)=I+\frac{2s_0}{1-s_0^2}\BH(s_0)^{-1}A$.

nodes.name: Setup notation
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a tree as in the lemma statement, $A$ its adjacency matrix, and $J = \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}$ the corresponding interaction matrix. Also set $D_H$ be the (diagonal) degree matrix of $H$.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Fix $H$, $A$, $J$, and the degree matrix $D_H$.

nodes.name: Localization plan
nodes.statement: To prove this, we shall once again use \Cref{lem:entropic-stability}. The control matrix will be of the form $C = (J+E)^{1/2} \psdge 0$ for a non-negative diagonal matrix $E$. Due to the ferromagneticity of the system, $C^2$ has all non-negative entries. At time $0 \le t \le 1$, $J_t$ will have the form $(1-t) J - tE$ -- in particular, at time $t=1$, $\mu_t$ is almost surely a product distribution so $\MLSI(\mu_t) = \Omega(1/n)$.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Use entropic stability with control matrix $(J+E)^{1/2}$ ending in a product measure.

nodes.name: Goal: control-covariance norm
nodes.statement: In the context of \Cref{lem:entropic-stability}, our goal is to bound, for all external fields $h \in \R^n$, the operator norm \begin{equation} \norm*{C \cdot \Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C} \le \norm*{\Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C^2 }. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Need to bound $\|C\Cov C\|\le\|\Cov C^2\|$.

nodes.name: Control-covariance norm bound
nodes.statement: \norm*{C \cdot \Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C} \le \norm*{\Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C^2 }.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.label: eq:bethe-hessian-coincidence-1

nodes.name: Reduce to zero field and dominate
nodes.statement: By \Cref{cor:cov-ferro-external-psd} (using the matrix $C^2$), it suffices to bound the above for $h = 0$. For $h = 0$, we recall that if $A^{(\ell)}$ is the matrix where the $uv$-th entry is $1$ if $u$ and $v$ are distance exactly $\ell$ apart and $0$ otherwise, \[ \Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,0} \right) \le \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)^{\ell} A^{(\ell)} \] in the sense that the matrix on the right is entry-wise at least the matrix on the left. In particular, \begin{equation} \norm*{\Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C^2 } \le \norm*{ \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)^{\ell} A^{(\ell)} \cdot C^2 }. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $h=0$ and dominate by the distance-matrix series.

nodes.name: Entrywise domination by distance-matrix series
nodes.statement: \norm*{\Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C^2 } \le \norm*{ \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)^{\ell} A^{(\ell)} \cdot C^2 }.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.label: eq:bethe-hessian-coincidence-2

nodes.name: Bethe Hessian inverse
nodes.statement: For ease of notation, denote $s_0 = \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}$. Recalling \Cref{def:bethe-hessian}, set \[ \BH(s) = \frac{(D_H - I) s^2 - As + I}{1-s^2}, \] so by \Cref{fact:bethe-inverse}, \[ \BH\left( s_0 \right)^{-1} = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)^\ell A^{(\ell)}. \]
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: The series equals $\BH(s_0)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Choose control matrix
nodes.statement: We choose \begin{align} C = \left((1-s_0^2) \cdot \BH\left( - s_0 \right)\right)^{1/2} . \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests

nodes.name: Bethe Hessian control matrix
nodes.statement: C = \left((1-s_0^2) \cdot \BH\left( - s_0 \right)\right)^{1/2} .
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.label: eq:control-matrix-tree-mlsi

nodes.name: Cancellation identity
nodes.statement: Now, \begin{align*} \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \left( \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}} \right)^{\ell} A^{(\ell)} \cdot C^2 &= (1-s_0^2) \cdot \BH\left( s_0 \right)^{-1} \cdot \BH\left( -s_0 \right) \\ &= (1-s_0^2) \cdot \BH(s_0)^{-1} \cdot \left( \BH(s_0) + \frac{2s_0}{1-s_0^2} \cdot A \right) \\ &= (1-s_0^2) \cdot I + 2 s_0 \cdot \BH(s_0)^{-1} \cdot A. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Product simplifies to $(1-s_0^2)I+2s_0\BH(s_0)^{-1}A$.

nodes.name: Bound the product
nodes.statement: Using the third bound in \Cref{lem:tree-cov} with \eqref{eq:bethe-hessian-coincidence-1} and \eqref{eq:bethe-hessian-coincidence-2}, we get the desired claim that \begin{align*} \norm*{C \cdot \Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J,h} \right) \cdot C} &\le \norm*{ (1-s_0^2) \cdot I + 2 s_0 \cdot \BH(s_0)^{-1} \cdot A } \\ &\le 1 + \frac{8}{(1-\gamma)^2} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Get $\|C\Cov C\|\le1+\frac{8}{(1-\gamma)^2}\frac\Delta D$.

nodes.name: Conclude MLSI
nodes.statement: Given that the product measure obtained at time $1$ satisfies an MLSI with constant $1/n$, it follows by \Cref{lem:entropic-stability,thm:anneal} that \begin{align*} \MLSI(\mu_{J,h}) &\ge \frac{1}{n} \cdot \exp\left( - \int_{0}^{1} \sup_{h \in \R^n} \norm*{ C \cdot \Cov\left( \mu_{(1-t)J, h} \right) \cdot C } \,dt \right) \\ &\ge \frac{1}{n} \cdot \exp\left( - \left( 1 + \frac{8}{(1-\gamma)^2} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D} \right) \right) = \frac{1}{ne^{O(\Delta)}} \end{align*} as desired.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Entropic stability and annealing give MLSI $1/(ne^{O(\Delta)})$.

nodes.name: Remarks on the choice of control matrix
nodes.statement: Before moving on, we make a handful of remarks about the above proof, specifically the choice of control matrix in \eqref{eq:control-matrix-tree-mlsi}: \begin{itemize} \item The choice is well-defined due to \Cref{cor:bethe-tree-psd}, which implies that $\BH\left(-s_0\right) \psdg 0$. \item It is important that we provide a negative argument to $\BH$ so that $C^2$ is equal to some positive scaling of the interaction matrix (which in turn is a scaling of the adjacency matrix because all the nonzero interactions are equal) plus a diagonal matrix -- this is required for stochastic localization to eventually kill the interaction matrix. Note that as a consequence of this, $C^2$ has all non-negative entries as desired. \item It is also important that the precise negative argument we provide is equal to $-s_0$ in order to be able to express $C^2$ as $\BH(s_0)$ plus some scaling of the adjacency matrix -- otherwise, there would also be a term corresponding to the degree matrix in the definition of the Bethe Hessian. This would cause issues in the methods we use to bound the operator norm. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: The Bethe Hessian control matrix is well defined and the argument $-s_0$ is needed so $C^2$ cancels the covariance.

nodes.name: MLSI for pseudorandom tree Ising models with signed interactions
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree on $n$ vertices, and $J$ an interaction matrix supported on $H$ with all interactions in $\left[- \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}, \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}\right]$. For any external field $h$, \[ \MLSI(\mu_{J,h}) \ge \frac{1}{ne^{O(\Delta)}}. \]
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
assumptions: Let $H$ be a $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom tree on $n$ vertices, and $J$ an interaction matrix supported on $H$ with all interactions in $\left[- \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}, \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}\right]$.
nodes.label: lem:pseudorandom-nonferro-mixing

nodes.name: Proof of signed tree MLSI
nodes.statement: This immediately follows using \Cref{lem:pseudorandom-ferro-mixing} in conjunction with \Cref{obs:sign-conjugation} and \Cref{lem:all-but-one-neg}, since $H$ is a tree.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Gauge transform to nonnegative interactions on the tree, then apply the ferromagnetic tree MLSI.

nodes.name: Proof of the near-forest MLSI
nodes.statement:
As remarked earlier, by \Cref{fact:mlsi-product}, it suffices to prove an MLSI of $\Omega\left( rac{1}{|C|e^{\Delta}}ight)$ for each component $C$ of $H$, which is a near-tree. Let $\mu$ be the corresponding Ising model on this component, with interaction matrix $estr{J}{C}$ and external field $estr{h}{C}$. Let $T$ be an arbitrary spanning tree of $C$ (which must also be $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom), and $
u$ the Ising model supported on $T$ with the same interaction strengths as in $\mu$. Observe that because $C$ has at most one edge in addition to those in $T$, and the interaction strengths are bounded by $ rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}$ in absolute value, we have \[ e^{- rac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}} \le  rac{\mu(\sigma)}{
u(\sigma)} \le e^{ rac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}}. \] Furthermore, $
u$ satisfies an MLSI by \Cref{lem:pseudorandom-nonferro-mixing}, so \Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate} completes the proof.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Tensorize over components, compare each near-tree to a spanning tree by Holley-Stroock, and apply the tree MLSI.

nodes.name: Tensorize over components
nodes.statement: As remarked earlier, by \Cref{fact:mlsi-product}, it suffices to prove an MLSI of $\Omega\left(\frac{1}{|C|e^{\Delta}}\right)$ for each component $C$ of $H$, which is a near-tree.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to prove the MLSI for each near-tree component.

nodes.name: Spanning tree comparison model
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be the corresponding Ising model on this component, with interaction matrix $\restr{J}{C}$ and external field $\restr{h}{C}$. Let $T$ be an arbitrary spanning tree of $C$ (which must also be $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom), and $\nu$ the Ising model supported on $T$ with the same interaction strengths as in $\mu$.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Define $\mu$ on the component and $\nu$ on a spanning tree.

nodes.name: Density ratio
nodes.statement: Observe that because $C$ has at most one edge in addition to those in $T$, and the interaction strengths are bounded by $\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}$ in absolute value, we have \[ e^{-\frac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}} \le \frac{\mu(\sigma)}{\nu(\sigma)} \le e^{\frac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{D}}}. \]
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Densities differ by at most $e^{2\gamma/\sqrt D}$.

nodes.name: Holley-Stroock transfer
nodes.statement: Furthermore, $\nu$ satisfies an MLSI by \Cref{lem:pseudorandom-nonferro-mixing}, so \Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate} completes the proof.
nodes.section: 4.5 MLSI for Ising models on pseudorandom near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the tree MLSI to $\mu$.

nodes.name: MLSI for centered SBM Ising models
nodes.statement: Fix constants $d > 1, \lambda \geq 0$. There exists a universal constant $\beta > 0$ such that the following is true. Let $\ol{A}_{\bG} \coloneqq A_{\bG} - \E[A_{\bG}|\bsigma]$ be the centered adjacency matrix of $\bG \sim \SBM(n, d, \lambda)$. nodes.name: Proof of MLSI for perturbed Ising models
nodes.statement: We can sample a uniform index $i$ from $[n]$ by the following two-step process. First, sample $b$ from a certain distribution $\calD$ on $\{C_1,\dots,C_m\}\cup\{v_1,\dots,v_{m'}\}$, and then choose $i$ as a uniformly random vertex from $b$. In particular, the distribution $\calD$ is defined as: \[ \Pr[b = v_i] = \frac{1}{n} \qquad \qquad \Pr[b = C_i] = \frac{|C_i|}{n}. \] For any $b$, and any pinning $x_{-b}$ to the spins outside of $b$, the resulting conditional distribution on $x_b$ is an Ising model with interaction matrix $(J+E)_b$ and some external field $h\parens*{x_{-b}}$ depending on the pinning. This lets us write the distribution $\mu$ as a mixture: \[ \mu = \E_{b\sim\calD} \E_{x_{-b}\sim\mu_{-b}} \mu_{(J+E)_b, h\parens*{x_{-b}}}\mper \] We can succinctly express the mixture distribution as $\rho$, the pair $(b, x_{-b})$ as $\bz$, and the resulting Ising model as $\pi_{\bz}$. To prove the MLSI, we write the following chain of inequalities. For any function $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\R_{\ge 0}$: \begin{align*} \calE_{\mu}(f, \log f) &\ge \E_{\bz\sim\rho} \calE_{\pi_{\bz}}(f, \log f) \\ &\ge \exp\parens*{-O\parens*{\eta \cdot n^{2\theta}}} \cdot \zeta \cdot \E_{\bz\sim\rho} \Ent_{\pi_{\bz}}[f] \tag*{\text{(MLSI for $\pi_{\bz}$, \Cref{lem:perturb-mlsi-centered})}}\\ &= \exp\parens*{-O\parens*{\eta \cdot n^{2\theta}}} \cdot \zeta \cdot \E_{b\sim\calD} \E_{x_{-b}\sim\mu_{-b}} \Ent_{\pi_{(b,x_{-b})}}[f] \\ &\ge \exp\parens*{-O\parens*{\eta \cdot n^{2\theta}}} \cdot \zeta \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\delta}{\eta n}\right) \cdot \E_{b\sim\{C_1,\dots,C_m\}\cup\{v_1,\dots,v_{m'}\}} \E_{x_{-b}\sim\mu_{-b}} \Ent_{\pi_{(b,x_{-b})}}[f] \\ &\ge \exp\parens*{-O\parens*{\eta \cdot n^{2\theta}}} \cdot \frac{\zeta}{n^{\frac{1}{1-2\sqrt{\delta}}}} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\delta}{\eta n}\right) \cdot \Ent_{\mu}[f], \tag*{(\Cref{cor:entropy-conservation-perturb})} \end{align*} where in the fourth line we move from $\calD$ to the uniform distribution over the parts using the fact that for any component $C_i$, \[ \frac{|C_i|/n}{1/(m+m')} \ge \frac{m}{n} \ge \frac{n - \sum_{i : |C_i| > 1} |C_i|}{n} \ge 1 - \frac{\delta}{\eta n}. \] This completes the proof.

Then $\mu_{J_{R}}$ satisfies \Cref{ass:parameters} with $m' \le n$ and \begin{align*} (\eta, \delta, \theta, \zeta) \leftarrow (\tfrac{2d}{n}, 8\alpha d^2, \tfrac{c\log(d(1+\eps))}{\eps^3 d}, n^{-o_d(1)}), \end{align*} where $c$ is a positive universal constant. Consequently, for $\eps = \Omega(\log d/d)^{1/3}$, Glauber dynamics on $\mu_{J_R}$ satisfies \[ \MLSI(\mu_{J_R}) \ge \frac{1}{n^{1 + o_d(1)}}\mper \]

assumptions: Let $\bG \sim \SBM(n, d, \lambda)$.

nodes.name: Proof of parameter verification for sparse SBMs
nodes.statement: Let $\cc(H)$ denote the connected components of $H$, and write $H = \sqcup_{C \in \cc(H)} C$. Let $\calS = \{C \in \cc(H): \abs{C} > 1\}$ be the nontrivial connected components, and $\calT = \{C \in \cc(H): \abs{C} = 1\}$ be the isolated vertices. In our setup, the error $E_H + E$ has entries whose magnitude are bounded by $\frac{d}{n}\left(1 + \frac{\abs{\lambda}}{\sqrt{d}}\right) \le \frac{2d}{n}$. On the other hand, \Cref{lem:component-size} implies that $\abs{\calS} \le \alpha n$, where $\alpha = \exp(-c\eps^3 d)$, and we trivially have $\abs{\calT} \le n$. Hence, we will verify the conditions for $\eta = \frac{2d}{n}$ and $m' = n$. Plugging these parameters in, we need $\delta$ to satisfy \begin{align*} \frac{2 d}{n} \cdot \sum_{C \in \calS} \abs{C}^2 &< \delta \\ 2 \cdot \left(\frac{2d}{n}\right)^2 \cdot n \cdot \sum_{C \in \calS} \abs{C}^2 &< \delta. \end{align*} Applying \Cref{lem:component-size} again, we see that the above inequalities are satisfied for $\delta > 8\alpha d^2$. Hence, we pick $\delta = 8\alpha d^2$, and we easily compute $1 - \frac{\delta}{\eta n} = 1 - 4\alpha d = 1 - o_d(1)$. Turning now to $\theta$, we need $\theta$ to satisfy \[ \max_{C \in \calS} \abs{C} \le n^{\theta}. \] \Cref{lem:single-component-bound} implies that we can take $\theta = \frac{c\log(d(1+\eps))}{\eps^3 d} = o_d(1)$ for some positive constant $c$. Next, by the proof of \Cref{thm:mlsi-bdd-growth-tree}, we can take $\zeta = n^{-\theta - o_n(1)} = n^{-o_d(1)}$ (observe that we get $n^{-\theta-o(1)}$ instead of $n^{-1-o(1)}$ here because we are considering the Ising model over $\{ \pm 1\}^{V(C_i)}$ instead of $\{\pm 1\}^n$). Finally, plugging these parameters into \Cref{lem:mlsi-under-assumptions}, we have \[ \exp(-O(\eta \cdot n^{2\theta})) = 1 - O\left(\frac{d}{n^{1-2\theta}}\right) \] By picking the constant factor in $\eps$ large enough, we can ensure that $\theta$ is sufficiently small so that the above term is $1 - o_n(1)$.
nodes.section: 5.3 MLSI for Ising models on perturbed near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Plug component-size bounds into the assumption and choose $\eta=2d/n$, $\delta=8\alpha d^2$, $\theta$, $\zeta$.

nodes.name: Proof of centered entropy conservation (reduction part)
nodes.statement: Let $B,H$ be a $(\Delta, D)$-decomposition as guaranteed by \Cref{lem:random-graph-decomposition}. As before, we will use \Cref{lem:interaction-sum-cov-bound} with \[ M_1 = (1-t)J_B + \theta I_B + \frac{\rho}{\Delta} I_{H \setminus \partial H} \quad \text{ and } M_2 = J_R, \] where we can take $\theta = \frac{t}{2} + \eta + 2\beta(1+\eps)$ due to \Cref{lem:bulk-spectral-radius} and $\rho$ as in the proof of \Cref{thm:entropy-conservation}. As before, we can reduce to the case $t=0$. Moreover, since $J_B$ is only supported on the bulk, one can follow the proof of \Cref{thm:entropy-conservation} to argue that to bound $\Cov(\mu_{M_1 + M_2, h})$, one only needs to bound covariances of Ising models on $M_2$. Namely, it suffices to establish the following PSD upper bounds for arbitrary external field $h'$: \begin{align*} \left\| \Cov\left( \mu_{M_2,h'} \right)_B \right\| &\le O(1) \\ \left\|\Cov(\mu_{M_2,h'})_H\right\| &\le O\left(\frac{\Delta}{D}\right). \end{align*} The main difficulty stems from the fact that $M_2 = J_R$ has support outside $H$; it is now supported on the complete graph on $H$, as well as the edges between $B$ and $H$.
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Reduce, as for the spin glass, to bounding covariances of Ising models with interactions $J_R$ on the bulk and near-forest.

nodes.statement:
Suppose that $
u$ is a distribution on a product domain $\calP = \calP_1 	imes \cdots 	imes \calP_k$, and let $\PI(
u)$ be the Poincar'{e} constant for Glauber dynamics on $
u$. Then for any $f : \calP 	o \R$, we have \[ \Var_
u(f) \le  rac{1}{k \cdot \PI(
u)} \sum_{i \in [k]} \E_{y_{-i}} \Var_{y_i | y_{-i}}(f). \]

nodes.name: Optimal Poincare constant for block dynamics
nodes.statement: We claim that the block Glauber dynamics studied in \Cref{sec:perturbed-near-forest} has an optimal Poincar\'{e} constant.

conclusions: the block Glauber dynamics studied in \Cref{sec:perturbed-near-forest} has an optimal Poincar\'{e} constant

nodes.name: Proof of the optimal Poincare constant
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Bound the block influence matrix by $\exp(-\Omega(\eps^3 d))$ and apply Hayes' spectral Dobrushin mixing bound.

nodes.name: Bound the block influence matrix
nodes.statement: In particular, for us $k = m + m'$ is the total number of connected components of $H$ (including isolated vertices). Indeed, due to \Cref{lem:parameter-dep,cor:dobrushin}, we have \begin{align*} \norm{\dobinf_{\nu}} &\le 8\alpha d^2 + \sqrt{8\alpha d^2} \\ &\le \exp(-\Omega(\eps^3 d)) \tag*{(\Cref{lem:component-size})}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Influence norm is $\exp(-\Omega(\eps^3d))$.

nodes.name: Hayes' lemma
nodes.statement: We now have the following lemma from \cite{Hay06}. \begin{lemma}[\cite{Hay06}] If the influence matrix of a distribution $\nu$ is bounded as $\|\calR_{\nu}\| < 1-\eps$, the mixing time of Glauber dynamics is $O((n \log n)/\eps)$. \end{lemma}
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Spectral Dobrushin condition gives fast mixing.

nodes.name: Spectral Dobrushin condition implies fast mixing
nodes.statement: If the influence matrix of a distribution $\nu$ is bounded as $\|\calR_{\nu}\| < 1-\eps$, the mixing time of Glauber dynamics is $O((n \log n)/\eps)$.
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
assumptions: If the influence matrix of a distribution $\nu$ is bounded as $\|\calR_{\nu}\| < 1-\eps$
conclusions: the mixing time of Glauber dynamics is $O((n \log n)/\eps)$

nodes.name: Poincare constant
nodes.statement: In conjunction with the previous equations, this implies an optimal mixing time bound for the block dynamics, and thus an $\Omega\left(\frac{1}{k}\right)$ bound on $\PI(\nu)$.
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Optimal mixing gives $\PI(\nu)=\Omega(1/k)$.

nodes.name: Removing weak interactions by perturbation
nodes.statement: Next, we justify the transfer from $\mu_{M_C+E_C, h}$ to $\mu_{M_C, h}$, thereby removing the pesky additional weak interactions $E_C$. To accomplish this, we will use the simple perturbation bound \Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate}. Indeed, we already proved such a density bound for perturbed Ising models in \Cref{lem:perturb-mlsi-centered}. Plugging in the explicit parameters for SBMs, as we did in the proof of \Cref{lem:parameter-dep}, we see that we can take $c = 1 + o_n(1)$ in \Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate}. In other words, we barely incur any loss transferring to $M_C$.
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Holley-Stroock with $c=1+o(1)$ lets one drop the weak $E_C$ interactions in each component.

nodes.name: Proof of centered entropy conservation (covariance bounds)
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Poincare inequality over components, perturbation to $M_C$, then near-forest covariance bounds on each component for $S=B$ and $S=H$.

nodes.name: Poincare and perturbation chain
nodes.statement: By \Cref{fact:var-cov}, if $v \in \R^n$ is a unit norm vector supported on $S \subseteq [n]$, then there is a positive constant $c > 0$ such that \begin{align*} \Vart_{x \sim \mu_{M_R, h'}}(\angles{v, x}) &\le c \sum_{C \in \cc(H)} \E_{x_{-C}} \Vart_{x \sim \mu_{M_C + E_C, h(x_{-C})}}(\angles{v_C, x_C}) \tag*{(\text{\Cref{lem:poincare}})}\\ &\le c(1+o_n(1)) \sum_{C \in \cc(H)} \E_{x_{-C}} \Vart_{x \sim \mu_{M_C, h(x_{-C})}}(\angles{v_C, x_C}) \tag*{(\text{\Cref{lem:mlsi-bdd-density-relate}})} \\ &\le c(1+o_n(1)) \sum_{C \in \cc(H)} \norm{v_C}^2 \E_{x_{-C}} \left[ \norm{\Cov(\mu_{M_C, h(x_{-C})})_{S}}\right]\mper \tag*{(\text{$v$ supported on $S$})} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Bound the variance by per-component covariances of $\mu_{M_C,\cdot}$.

nodes.name: Interaction range
nodes.statement: Recall that $M_H = \frac{\beta}{\sqrt{d}}(\ol{A}_H \circ A_H)$. Since the centering interaction is $O(\frac{d}{n})$, it follows that the interactions are in $\left[ -\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{d}} , \frac{\beta}{\sqrt{d}} \right] = \left[ - \frac{\beta\sqrt{1+\eps}}{\sqrt{d(1+\eps)}} , \frac{\beta\sqrt{1+\eps}}{\sqrt{d(1+\eps)}} \right]$, so we can apply \Cref{lem:near-forest-cov} with $\gamma = \beta\sqrt{1+\eps}$.
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Interactions lie in $[-\beta/\sqrt d,\beta/\sqrt d]$, so apply the near-forest covariance lemma with $\gamma=\beta\sqrt{1+\eps}$.

nodes.name: Bulk and near-forest bounds
nodes.statement: Taking $S = B$ and applying \Cref{lem:near-forest-cov} uniformly on each component $C$ yields \begin{align*} \norm{\Cov(\mu_{M_R, h'})_B} \le c(1+o(1)) \cdot \left(\frac{e^{2\beta/\sqrt{d}}}{(1-\beta\sqrt{1+\eps})^2}\right), \end{align*} and for $S = H$ we obtain that \begin{align*} \norm{\Cov(\mu_{M_R, h'})_H} \le c(1+o(1)) \cdot \left(\frac{e^{2\beta/\sqrt{d}}}{(1-\beta\sqrt{1+\eps})^2} \right) \cdot \frac{\Delta}{D} . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: Covariance bounds on $B$ and $H$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By following the same calculations as in \Cref{thm:main-mixing}, the upshot is that for sufficiently small (constant) $\beta > 0$, we have for some constant $C$ independent of $\Delta$ that \begin{align*} \Cov(\mu_{(1-t)J_B + J_R, h}) \psdle C \left( I_B + \Delta I_{H \setminus \partial H} \right), \end{align*} as desired.
nodes.section: 5.4 Entropy conservation for centered stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: As for the spin glass, get the PSD bound.

nodes.name: Excision of a graph
nodes.statement: For a graph $G$, and for each vertex $v\in V(G)$, define $N_\ell(v)$ to be the set of vertices at distance exactly $\ell$ from $v$ and $B_\ell(v)$ to be the induced subgraph on $G$ on those vertices within distance $\ell$ of $v$. We say that $v$ is \emph{$\ell$-heavy} if $|B_\ell(v)| > (d(1+\eps))^\ell$, and conversely that $v$ is \emph{$\ell$-light} if $|B_{\ell}(v)| \le (d(1+\eps))^{\ell}$, and set \[ \ell(v) = \min\{ \ell \ge 0 : v \text{ is $L$-light for all $L \ge \ell$} \}. \] Note in particular that if $|B_L(v)| \le (d(1+\eps))^L$ for all $L \ge 0$, then $\ell(v) = 0$ and $B_{\ell(v)}(v)$ has no edges. Finally, we define the \emph{excision} of a graph $G$ as \[ H \coloneqq \bigcup_{v \in V} B_{\ell(v)}(v), \] and refer to the graph after the removal of edges in $H$ as the \emph{bulk} of $G$.
nodes.section: 6 Near-forest decomposition for stochastic block models
nodes.statement_short: $\ell(v)$ is the least radius beyond which $v$'s balls stay below $(d(1+\eps))^\ell$; the excision is the union of balls $B_{\ell(v)}(v)$.

nodes.name: Bulk has bounded degree and excision is pseudorandom
nodes.statement: For any graph $G$, let $G_1$ and $G_2$ denote its bulk and excision respectively. Then, for some $\Delta > 0$ and $D \coloneqq (1+\eps)d$: \begin{enumerate} \item The maximum degree of $G_1$ is at most $D$. \item $G_2$ is $(\Delta,D)$-pseudorandom with respect to $S\coloneqq V'(G_1)\cap V'(G_2)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof that the excision is a near-forest
nodes.statement: Condition on the event in \Cref{lem:components-diam}, so we have that every component $C$ of $H$ has diameter at most $\log n/d$. Suppose instead that $C$ had tree-excess at least $2$, and let $C_1,C_2$ be minimal cycles in $C$ (in that they do not have any chords). Consider the induced subgraph on the set $S$ of vertices in $C$ comprised of $C_1,C_2$, and a shortest path (in $C$) between the two. Note in particular that $S$ is connected, and $|S| \le 5 \diam(C)$. Since $\eps = \Omega_d(\log d/d)^{1/3}$, we may apply \Cref{lem:small-subgraphs-have-excess-1} to conclude that the tree-excess of the induced subgraph on $S$ is at most $1$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Cluster graph
nodes.statement: Given a graph $G$ on $[n]$, the associated \emph{cluster graph} $\Cluster(G)$ has vertex set $[n]$, with an edge between $u$ and $v$ iff $\ell(u),\ell(v) > 0$ and $B_{\ell(u)}(u) \cap B_{\ell(v)}(v) \ne \emptyset$. Furthermore, each vertex $u$ in this graph has associated weight $\wtt(u) = (1+\eps)^{\ell(u)}$, and each edge $uv$ has weight $\wtt(u, v) = \ell(u)+\ell(v)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Vertices with $\ell(u)>0$ are adjacent iff their heavy balls intersect; weights $(1+\eps)^{\ell(u)}$ and $\ell(u)+\ell(v)$.
nodes.label: def:cluster-graph

nodes.name: Proof of the excision diameter bound
nodes.statement: Observe that \Cref{lem:components-diam} follows immediately from the following two statements: \begin{enumerate} \item \Cref{lem:no-tree-excess-cluster-graph}, which shows that if a connected component of $\bH$ has large diameter, then it causes a high-weight induced path in $\Cluster(\bG)$. \item \Cref{lem:no-long-path-cluster}, which establishes that there are no high-weight induced paths in $\Cluster(\bG)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Large diameter forces a heavy induced path in the cluster graph, which whp does not exist.

nodes.name: Two ingredients
nodes.statement: Observe that \Cref{lem:components-diam} follows immediately from the following two statements:
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: The diameter bound follows from two lemmas.

nodes.name: Large diameter gives heavy path
nodes.statement: \Cref{lem:no-tree-excess-cluster-graph}, which shows that if a connected component of $\bH$ has large diameter, then it causes a high-weight induced path in $\Cluster(\bG)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Large diameter forces a heavy induced path.

nodes.name: No heavy paths
nodes.statement: \Cref{lem:no-long-path-cluster}, which establishes that there are no high-weight induced paths in $\Cluster(\bG)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Heavy induced paths do not exist whp.

nodes.name: Large diameter yields a heavy induced path in the cluster graph
nodes.statement: Suppose the diameter of a connected component of $\bH$ exceeds $\tau$. Then there are vertices $u_1,\dots, u_k\in[n]$ such that the induced subgraph in $\Cluster(\bG)$ is the path $u_1\dots u_k$, and \[ \sum_{i\in[k]} \ell(u_i) \ge \frac{\tau}{2}\mper \]
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
assumptions: Suppose the diameter of a connected component of $\bH$ exceeds $\tau$.
conclusions: Then there are vertices $u_1,\dots, u_k\in[n]$ such that the induced subgraph in $\Cluster(\bG)$ is the path $u_1\dots u_k$
nodes.label: lem:no-tree-excess-cluster-graph

nodes.name: No heavy induced paths in the cluster graph
nodes.statement: Define $\eta$ as $\min\left\{\frac{\eps^2}{54}, \frac{1}{18}\right\}$. With probability $1-o(1)$, for any $U = \{u_1,\dots,u_k\}$ such that the induced subgraph on $U$ in $\Cluster(\bG)$ is the path $u_1\dots u_k$, we have: \[ \sum_{i\in[k]} \ell(u_i) < \frac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}\mper \]
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
assumptions: Define $\eta$ as $\min\left\{\frac{\eps^2}{54}, \frac{1}{18}\right\}$.
conclusions: With probability $1-o(1)$, for any $U = \{u_1,\dots,u_k\}$ such that the induced subgraph on $U$ in $\Cluster(\bG)$ is the path $u_1\dots u_k$, we have:
nodes.label: lem:no-long-path-cluster

nodes.name: Proof that large diameter yields a heavy induced path
nodes.statement: There must be vertices $a$ and $b$ in a single connected component of $\bH$ such that $\dist_{\bH}(a,b) > \tau$. Let $u$ and $v$ be vertices such that $B_{\ell(a)}(a)$ and $B_{\ell(b)}(b)$ contain $u$ and $v$ respectively. Let $u_1u_2\dots u_k$ be the weighted shortest path between $u$ and $v$ in $\Cluster(\bG)$ where $u_1 = u$ and $u_k = v$. The path between $a$ and $b$ has length bounded by $2\sum_{i\in[k]}\ell_i$, and hence: \[ \sum_{i\in[k]} \ell_i \ge \frac{\tau}{2}\mper \] The induced subgraph on $\{u_1,\dots,u_k\}$ certainly contains the claimed path by construction. It remains to show that there are no other edges besides the ones in the path. If there is an edge between $u_i$ and $u_j$ for $j\ne i\pm 1$ for $i < j$, then the path $u_1\cdots u_i u_j u_{j+1} \cdots u_k$ is a shorter path than the original one, which leads to a contradiction. Indeed, since the edge weights are positive and $\wtt(u, v) = \ell(u) + \ell(v)$, any path between $u_i$ and $u_j$, in particular $u_i u_{i+1} \cdots u_{j-1} u_j$, has weight at least $\ell(u_i) + \ell(u_j)$, with equality if and only if the path is just the edge $u_iu_j$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Take a weighted shortest path in the cluster graph between balls containing far-apart vertices; shortcuts would contradict minimality.

nodes.name: Far-apart vertices and covering balls
nodes.statement: There must be vertices $a$ and $b$ in a single connected component of $\bH$ such that $\dist_{\bH}(a,b) > \tau$. Let $u$ and $v$ be vertices such that $B_{\ell(a)}(a)$ and $B_{\ell(b)}(b)$ contain $u$ and $v$ respectively.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Pick $a,b$ at distance $>\tau$ and vertices $u,v$ of balls containing them.

nodes.name: Shortest path weight
nodes.statement: Let $u_1u_2\dots u_k$ be the weighted shortest path between $u$ and $v$ in $\Cluster(\bG)$ where $u_1 = u$ and $u_k = v$. The path between $a$ and $b$ has length bounded by $2\sum_{i\in[k]}\ell_i$, and hence: \[ \sum_{i\in[k]} \ell_i \ge \frac{\tau}{2}\mper \]
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: The path has total radius at least $\tau/2$.

nodes.name: Path is contained
nodes.statement: The induced subgraph on $\{u_1,\dots,u_k\}$ certainly contains the claimed path by construction.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: The induced subgraph contains the path.

nodes.name: No chords remain
nodes.statement: It remains to show that there are no other edges besides the ones in the path.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Need no extra edges.

nodes.name: Chord gives shorter path
nodes.statement: If there is an edge between $u_i$ and $u_j$ for $j\ne i\pm 1$ for $i < j$, then the path $u_1\cdots u_i u_j u_{j+1} \cdots u_k$ is a shorter path than the original one, which leads to a contradiction. Indeed, since the edge weights are positive and $\wtt(u, v) = \ell(u) + \ell(v)$, any path between $u_i$ and $u_j$, in particular $u_i u_{i+1} \cdots u_{j-1} u_j$, has weight at least $\ell(u_i) + \ell(u_j)$, with equality if and only if the path is just the edge $u_iu_j$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: A chord would contradict minimality of the weighted shortest path.

nodes.name: Violating set and minimal violating set
nodes.statement: We say a subset of vertices $U$ is a \emph{violating set} if the induced subgraph on $U$ in $\Cluster(\bG)$ is a path of weight exceeding $\tfrac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}$. We say $U$ is a \emph{minimal violating set} if it is a violating set, and no subset of $U$ is a violating set.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests

nodes.name: Signature of a minimal violating set
nodes.statement: The \emph{signature} of a minimum violating set is the tuple $\parens*{k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}}$ where $k$ is the number of vertices in the minimum violating set, $\vec{u} = (u_1,\dots,u_k)$ is the vertices in the minimum violating set in the order they appear in the path, and $\vec{\ell} = (\ell(u_1),\dots,\ell(u_k))$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests

nodes.name: Signature class $\calS_\kappa$
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $\kappa$, define $\calS_{\kappa}$ as all signatures $({k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}})$ for which $k\ge 1$ and $\vec{\ell}$ is in $[\kappa]^{k}$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests

nodes.name: Violating sets contain minimal violating sets
nodes.statement: If $U\subseteq[n]$ is a violating set in $\Cluster(\bG)$, then it contains a minimal violating set $U'\subseteq U$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
assumptions: If $U\subseteq[n]$ is a violating set in $\Cluster(\bG)$
conclusions: it contains a minimal violating set $U'\subseteq U$
nodes.label: obs:min-violating-set

nodes.name: Union bound on minimal violating sets
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $\kappa$, the probability that $\Cluster(\bG)$ contains a minimal violating set is bounded by \[ \sum_{\parens*{k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}}\in\calS_{\kappa}} \Pr\bracks*{\exists\text{MVS with signature }\parens*{k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}}\text{ in }\Cluster\parens*{\bG} } + \Pr\bracks*{\exists v\in[n]\text{ s.t. }\ell(v) > \kappa}, \] where MVS is short for ``minimal violating set''.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
assumptions: For any positive integer $\kappa$
conclusions: the probability that $\Cluster(\bG)$ contains a minimal violating set is bounded by
nodes.label: obs:MVS-bound

nodes.name: Heaviness radius bound
nodes.statement: For $\kappa = \frac{4}{\eps}\log\frac{\log n}{\eta d}$, we have: \[ \Pr\bracks*{\exists v\in[n]\text{ s.t. }\ell(v)>\kappa} = o(1)\mper \]
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
assumptions: For $\kappa = \frac{4}{\eps}\log\frac{\log n}{\eta d}$
nodes.label: lem:radius-bound

nodes.name: Probability bound for a single signature
nodes.statement: For $\kappa = \frac{4}{\eps}\log\frac{\log n}{\eta d}$ and for any $(k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell})\in\calS_{\kappa}$ where $\vec{\ell} = (\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k)$, we have: \begin{align*} \Pr&\bracks*{\exists\text{MVS with signature }\parens*{k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}} \text{ in }\Cluster(\bG) } \\ &\qquad\le \frac{1}{n^{k-1}}\prod_{i\in[k]} 2\ell_i^2\cdot\parens*{d(1+\eps)}^{2\ell_i}\cdot\exp\parens*{-\frac{\eta d}{2}\parens*{1+\frac{\eps}{4}}^{\ell_i}}\mper \end{align*}
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
assumptions: For $\kappa = \frac{4}{\eps}\log\frac{\log n}{\eta d}$ and for any $(k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell})\in\calS_{\kappa}$ where $\vec{\ell} = (\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k)$
nodes.statement_short: An MVS with given signature has probability at most $n^{-(k-1)}\prod_i 2\ell_i^2(d(1+\eps))^{2\ell_i}e^{-\frac{\eta d}{2}(1+\eps/4)^{\ell_i}}$.
nodes.label: lem:single-signature-bound

nodes.name: Interpretation of the signature bound
nodes.statement: The way to interpret the above is to think of the probability bound as decaying at a \emph{doubly} exponential rate in each $\ell_i$, and for the events $\{u_i\text{ is }\ell_i\text{-heavy}\}$ as being approximately independent. See \Cref{lem:ball-tail} and its proof to understand the doubly exponential decay rate.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests

nodes.name: Proof that the cluster graph has no heavy induced paths
nodes.statement: By \Cref{obs:min-violating-set} it suffices to prove that there is no minimal violating set in $\Cluster(\bG)$. The definition of a signature $\parens*{k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}}$ of a minimal violating set implies that $\sum_i\ell_i \ge \frac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}$. Hence, by \Cref{obs:MVS-bound,lem:radius-bound,lem:single-signature-bound}, we get that the probability of containing a violating set is at most: \begin{align} n \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ldots \ell_k \\ \sum \ell_i \ge \tfrac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}}} \prod_{i \in [k]} 2\ell_i^2 \cdot (d(1+\eps))^{2\ell_i} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right). \end{align} Consider one of the terms in the product, which is \[ \exp\left(\log(2\ell_i^2) + 2\ell_i \log (d(1+\eps)) - \frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right) \le \exp\left(\ell_i (2\log (d(1+\eps))+2) - \frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right). \] We claim that for \begin{equation} \eps \ge 1500 \left( \frac{100+\log d}{d} \right)^{1/3}, \end{equation} the above is at most $\exp \left( - \ell_i \left( 1 + \frac{\eta \eps d}{16} \right) \right)$. Indeed, since $\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i} \ge \frac{\eps}{4} \cdot \ell_i$, the above quantity is at most \[ \exp\left( - \ell_i \left( \frac{\eta \eps d}{8} - 2 - 2 \log\left( d (1+\eps) \right) \right) \right). \] Therefore, it suffices for $\eps$ to satisfy \[ \frac{\eta \eps d}{16} \ge 2 \log \left( d (1+\eps) \right) + 3. \] It is straightforward to verify that $\eps$ as in~\eqref{eq:eps-constraint-main} satisfies the above. Given this, \eqref{eq:long-path-prob} is at most \begin{align*} n \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ldots \ell_k \\ \sum \ell_i \ge \tfrac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}}} \exp\left(-\left(\frac{\eta\eps d}{16} + 1\right)\sum_{i \in [k]} \ell_i\right) & \le \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ldots \ell_k \\ \sum \ell_i \ge \tfrac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}}} \exp\left(-\sum_{i \in [k]} \ell_i\right) \\ &\le \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{\ell_1, \ldots \ell_k \ge 1} \exp\left(-\sum_{i \in [k]} \ell_i\right) \\ &\le \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k \ge 1} \exp(-\Omega(k)) = o(1), \end{align*} as desired.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over signatures using the single-signature bound; each factor decays as $e^{-\ell_i(1+\eta\eps d/16)}$ for large enough $\eps$.

nodes.name: Reduce to minimal violating sets
nodes.statement: By \Cref{obs:min-violating-set} it suffices to prove that there is no minimal violating set in $\Cluster(\bG)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Excisions of sparse random graphs are near-forests
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to rule out minimal violating sets.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: The definition of a signature $\parens*{k,\vec{u},\vec{\ell}}$ of a minimal violating set implies that $\sum_i\ell_i \ge \frac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}$. Hence, by \Cref{obs:MVS-bound,lem:radius-bound,lem:single-signature-bound}, we get that the probability of containing a violating set is at most: \begin{align} n \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ldots \ell_k \\ \sum \ell_i \ge \tfrac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}}} \prod_{i \in [k]} 2\ell_i^2 \cdot (d(1+\eps))^{2\ell_i} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right). \end{align}

nodes.statement_short: Combine union bound, radius bound and single-signature bound.

nodes.name: Union bound on violating sets
nodes.statement: n \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ldots \ell_k \\ \sum \ell_i \ge \tfrac{32\log n}{\eta\eps d}}} \prod_{i \in [k]} 2\ell_i^2 \cdot (d(1+\eps))^{2\ell_i} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right).

nodes.name: Single factor
nodes.statement: Consider one of the terms in the product, which is \[ \exp\left(\log(2\ell_i^2) + 2\ell_i \log (d(1+\eps)) - \frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right) \le \exp\left(\ell_i (2\log (d(1+\eps))+2) - \frac{\eta d}{2}\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i}\right). \]

nodes.name: Claim: factor decays for large $\eps$
nodes.statement: We claim that for \begin{equation} \eps \ge 1500 \left( \frac{100+\log d}{d} \right)^{1/3}, \end{equation} the above is at most $\exp \left( - \ell_i \left( 1 + \frac{\eta \eps d}{16} \right) \right)$. Indeed, since $\left(1+\frac{\eps}{4}\right)^{\ell_i} \ge \frac{\eps}{4} \cdot \ell_i$, the above quantity is at most \[ \exp\left( - \ell_i \left( \frac{\eta \eps d}{8} - 2 - 2 \log\left( d (1+\eps) \right) \right) \right). \] Therefore, it suffices for $\eps$ to satisfy \[ \frac{\eta \eps d}{16} \ge 2 \log \left( d (1+\eps) \right) + 3. \] It is straightforward to verify that $\eps$ as in~\eqref{eq:eps-constraint-main} satisfies the above.

nodes.statement: \eps \ge 1500 \left( \frac{100+\log d}{d} \right)^{1/3},
